passages.t: Tested in the wilderness: stones into bread
passages.happening:
Straight after his baptism, the Spirit leads Jesus out into the wilderness “to be tempted by the devil” (verse 1). He fasts, going without food, for forty days and forty nights, and at the end he is hungry.

Then the tempter comes. “If You are the Son of God, tell these stones to become bread” (verse 3). Jesus answers with Scripture: man does not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of God (verse 4).
passages.hearers:
The word translated ‘tempted’ also means ‘tested’. Both senses are here. The devil is trying to make Jesus fall. God, who led him there by the Spirit, is proving him true.

The devil's first words pick up the voice from heaven. In chapter 3 the Father said, ‘This is My beloved Son.’ Now the devil says, ‘If You are the Son of God.’ The test is about what kind of Son Jesus will be.

Forty would ring bells for any Jewish hearer. Israel wandered forty years in the wilderness. Moses was on the mountain forty days and nights without bread (Exodus 34:28). Elijah walked forty days and nights to the mountain of God (1 Kings 19:8).

And the Son in the wilderness would remind them of another son. God called Israel “My firstborn son” (Exodus 4:22). He led Israel through the water and into the desert to test them, and Israel grumbled for bread. Now the Son of God passes through the water of baptism into the desert, and he is hungry too.
passages.ot: All three of Jesus' answers in this chapter come from Deuteronomy 6 to 8, where Moses reminds Israel of their forty years in the wilderness. This first answer is Deuteronomy 8:3. Moses tells Israel that God let them go hungry and then fed them with manna, “so that you might understand that man does not live on bread alone, but on every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD.” Israel learned that lesson badly. Jesus lives it.
passages.hard:
Is the devil real, or a way of speaking about evil? Matthew presents him as a real power that speaks and acts, and so does the rest of the New Testament. Many modern readers find that hard to accept, and some Christians read the scene as an inward struggle told as a story. The historic church has read it as Matthew tells it. Either way, the tests are real ones: to use power for yourself, to force God's hand, to gain the world by bowing to the wrong master.

A word of care about fasting. Jesus' forty days were a unique moment. Christians have fasted in many ways, but no one should go without food in a way that harms the body. Ask a doctor first, and if not eating has become a struggle for you, please talk to someone you trust and a health professional.
passages.asks: The first test was to meet a real need, hunger, in a way that went around trusting the Father. Where are you tempted to take a shortcut to something good? And are God's words as necessary to you as food?

passages.happening:
The devil takes Jesus to Jerusalem and sets him on the highest point of the temple. If you are the Son of God, he says, throw yourself down. And now the devil quotes Scripture too: God will command his angels to catch you, so that you will not strike your foot against a stone (verse 6). Jesus answers, “Do not put the Lord your God to the test” (verse 7).

Then the devil takes him to a very high mountain and shows him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory. All this I will give you, he says, if you fall down and worship me. Jesus says, “Away from Me, Satan!” For it is written: worship the Lord your God and serve him only (verse 10).

The devil leaves him, and angels come and take care of him.
passages.hearers:
The temple was the centre of Jewish life, and Herod had rebuilt it on a vast scale. The ‘pinnacle’ means a wing or edge, some high point of the temple buildings. No one knows exactly which. Many think of the south-east corner of the great courts, which stood high above the Kidron Valley. A fall from there would mean death, unless God stepped in, in front of everyone. It would be a spectacular way to prove who he was.

The mountain test goes straight to the heart of the hope for a Messiah. Many hoped for a king who would take back the land and rule the nations. The devil offers Jesus exactly that, all at once, without a cross. The price is to bow to the wrong master.

Jesus will be on a mountain again at the end of the book. There he says, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me” (28:18). He receives from his Father, by way of the cross, what the devil offered him without it.
passages.ot:
The devil quotes Psalm 91:11-12, a psalm of trust that God protects those who shelter in him. He leaves out its heart, which is trust, and turns it into a dare. Jesus answers with Deuteronomy 6:16, “Do not test the LORD your God as you tested Him at Massah.” At Massah, Israel had demanded water and asked, “Is the LORD among us or not?” (Exodus 17:7). Trust does not need to make God prove himself.

The last answer is Deuteronomy 6:13, where Moses warns Israel not to follow other gods once they are rich and settled in the land. Israel often failed that test. Jesus does not.
passages.hard:
The devil can quote the Bible. That should make every reader careful. A verse pulled out of its place can be made to say almost anything, even to justify reckless or proud acts. Jesus does not answer by throwing a verse back; he answers with the meaning of the whole of Scripture, which calls us to trust God, not to test him.

Did the devil really have the world's kingdoms to give? Jesus does not argue the point. John's Gospel calls the devil the prince of this world (John 12:31), while insisting that the world finally belongs to God.
passages.asks: The last two tests offer a short cut: prove yourself, and gain everything, without suffering. Where are you tempted to make God prove himself before you will trust him? And what ‘kingdoms’ would you be tempted to bow down for?

passages.happening:
Jesus hears that John has been put in prison. He goes back to Galilee. He leaves his home town of Nazareth and goes to live in Capernaum, a town on the shore of the Sea of Galilee, in the old tribal lands of Zebulun and Naphtali.

Matthew sees a prophecy here, from Isaiah: the people living in darkness have seen a great light (verse 16).

“From that time on Jesus began to preach, ‘Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near’” (verse 17). It is the same message John preached.
passages.hearers:
Capernaum was a fishing town on the north-west shore of the lake, near where the Jordan River flows in. It became Jesus' home base, and Matthew later calls it ‘His own town’ (9:1).

Zebulun and Naphtali were two of Israel's twelve tribes, whose lands lay in the north. A Jewish hearer would remember what happened to them. Around 733 to 732 BC the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser III swept through Galilee and carried its people away captive (2 Kings 15:29). The north was the first part of Israel to fall into darkness.

‘Galilee of the Gentiles’ was not a compliment. Galilee was surrounded by non-Jewish lands and had many non-Jewish people living in and around it. To the people of Jerusalem it could seem a mixed, second-class region. Matthew says the light dawns first exactly there.

The line ‘From that time on Jesus began’ is a turning point in Matthew's book. It comes again only once, at 16:21, when Jesus begins to speak of the cross.
passages.ot: The quotation is Isaiah 9:1-2. Isaiah says that the land God once humbled, Zebulun and Naphtali, he will one day honour: “The people walking in darkness have seen a great light” (Isaiah 9:2). Hearers who knew Isaiah would know what comes next in that chapter: “For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given” (Isaiah 9:6), a son of David whose rule will have no end. Matthew is saying that the child of Isaiah 9 has come, and that his light begins in the region that was first to fall.
passages.asks: Jesus began in the place people looked down on, the first to be lost and the last to be expected. Where do you think the light of God is least likely to reach, in your town or in your own life? Matthew says that is exactly where it dawns first.

passages.happening:
Walking by the Sea of Galilee, Jesus sees two brothers, Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew. They are casting a net into the lake, because they are fishermen. “Come, follow Me,” Jesus says, “and I will make you fishers of men” (verse 19). At once they leave their nets and follow him.

A little further on he sees two more brothers, James and John, the sons of Zebedee. They are in a boat with their father, mending their nets. Jesus calls them, and they leave the boat and their father and follow him.
passages.hearers:
Fishing was a major trade around the lake. Boats were small wooden working boats; one from about Jesus' time, around eight metres long and patched many times, was found in the mud of the lake shore in 1986. These men were not poor beggars. They owned boats and nets and worked in family businesses. Mark adds that Zebedee had hired men (Mark 1:20).

Teachers in Jesus' day did have students. But usually a student chose his teacher and asked to learn from him. Here Jesus does the choosing, and he does not say ‘learn the law from me’. He says ‘follow Me’. The call is to him.

Leaving a father in the boat was a costly thing. In that world the family business and duty to your father were close to sacred. Matthew does not soften it. Following Jesus came first.
passages.ot: ‘Fishers of men’ may echo Jeremiah 16:16, where God says he will send for many fishermen to gather his people. In Jeremiah the picture is of judgment, of people being caught and brought in. Jesus turns it into rescue: these fishermen will gather people for God's kingdom.
passages.asks: Jesus did not ask these men to stop being who they were. Fishermen would still be fishers, now of people. What skills and habits of your ordinary work could Jesus use? And what nets, the things you hold onto, might he be asking you to leave?

passages.happening:
Jesus travels all over Galilee. He teaches in the synagogues, preaches the good news of the kingdom, and heals every kind of disease and sickness. News of him spreads through the whole of Syria. People bring him everyone who is ill: those in great pain, those troubled by demons, those who have seizures, and those who cannot move. And he heals them.

Huge crowds follow him, from Galilee, from the Decapolis, from Jerusalem and Judea, and from beyond the Jordan.
passages.hearers:
A synagogue was a local meeting place where Jews gathered on the Sabbath to read and explain the Scriptures and to pray. Any respected visitor could be invited to teach, which is how Jesus could speak in synagogue after synagogue.

Syria here means the Roman province to the north. The crowds come from every direction: from Jewish lands like Galilee and Judea, and from the Decapolis, the ‘ten cities’, a league of Greek towns mostly east of the Jordan where many non-Jews lived. Already, before the Sermon on the Mount, Matthew shows the crowds that will gather to hear it.

Notice the three things Jesus does: teaching, preaching and healing. Matthew uses almost the same words again at 9:35, and the two verses frame chapters 5 to 9. In between, Jesus teaches (the Sermon, chapters 5 to 7) and heals (ten miracles, chapters 8 and 9). The words and the works go together.
passages.hard: What does it mean that Jesus healed ‘every disease’? Matthew means that no illness was beyond him, not that every sick person in Galilee was healed. Christians today still pray for the sick, and many testify to healing. Many also live with illness that does not go away, and Matthew's Jesus never blames the sick for their sickness. To pray for healing and to see a doctor are not opposites; Christians have done both from the beginning.
passages.asks: Jesus' good news came in words and in care for bodies. Which do you find easier to give, words or practical help? Where could you do the one you usually leave out?
